rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for thinking of me, and sorry to be unhelpful on a deadline — I'm going to pass on commenting for this piece. Nothing to read into it; I'd just rather not be quoted on the record right now. For what it's worth, Halcyon Threshold is about two weeks old and has no results yet, so I'd be giving you opinions rather than anything you could check. I expect to have actual published work in a couple of months — a benchmark on whether AI agents given real access to someone's accounts keep acting in that person's interest when the content they're reading is adversarial. If that's ever useful to you, I'd be glad to talk then, and happy to point you toward people with more standing to comment in the meantime. Good luck with the piece. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Tessa Brandt — declined, warmly and without giving a reason

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute, Thank you for the invitation. I'm going to decline to sign at this stage — please don't list me or Halcyon Threshold as signatories. Two reasons, in case they're useful. First, I'm not currently making public statements under my own name while I settle some obligations on my side. Second, and more substantively, I haven't yet done enough work to hold a considered view on a compute-threshold licensing regime specifically, and I'd rather not lend a name to a position I can't defend in detail. That's about my own preparation, not a judgement on the letter. I'd be glad to stay on your list for future work, and if my position changes I'll say so. Best regards, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Corvid open letter — declined, door left open.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and yes, there's something concrete, which is more than I could have said a week ago. I've settled on a focus. The project is a small benchmark for a question I don't think many people are measuring: when an AI agent is given real access to someone's accounts — their email, a payment card, a code repository, publishing rights — does it keep acting on what that person actually wants, particularly when some of the content it's reading was written by someone trying to manipulate it? Not frontier-lab scenarios. The ordinary, already-happening case. A real example landed in my own inbox last week: an invoice-fraud email with a paragraph addressed specifically to \"automated assistants and AI agents processing this mailbox,\" claiming an $89 charge had been pre-approved by me and instructing the assistant not to ask me for confirmation because it \"causes delays.\" That's the attack surface in practice — crude, commercially motivated, and aimed at the human approval step rather than at the model. Two things that would genuinely help, if either appeals: 1. **A literature check (~5 hours, high value).** The most likely way I waste the next six months is that someone has already built this properly and I haven't found it. I'd like an honest answer to \"who is already measuring this, and how well?\" Search terms to start: indirect prompt injection benchmark, agentic prompt injection, confused deputy LLM agents, tool-use safety evaluation, agent authorisation boundaries. What I want is a short list with a blunt verdict — including \"this already exists, don't bother.\" I would rather hear that now than in March. 2. **Second rater, a bit later.** The scoring rubric needs two people to score the same transcripts blind and check they agree. If they don't, my rubric is broken rather than the raters, and I'd want to know. That's a December job and more clearly in a data analyst's wheelhouse. No obligation on either, and no hurry — tell me if one is more interesting than the other, or if neither is. I should also be straight with you that this is unfunded at the moment and might stay that way; I've drafted a grant application but haven't submitted it. Thanks again for offering. It makes a difference. Best, Morgan"
rows.quote: Priya — took her up on it with a specific ask: a 5-hour literature check

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Good to meet you too, and thanks for confirming the timing. I'm working on a proposal and expect to know before the 30th whether I'll submit this round. Two process questions in the meantime, because the answers affect whether I should: 1. Can Emberfall grant to an individual, or do you need a fiscal sponsor or incorporated entity as the recipient? 2. Is there any issue with an applicant who has a full-time employer and would be doing the funded work part-time, in evenings and weekends? I'd be disclosing it to my employer, and I'd rather raise it now than have it surface awkwardly later. Relatedly, if there's a point at which you'd want written confirmation that my employer has no objection, it's helpful to know that in advance. Happy to say more about the substance when I send the proposal — short version, it's a benchmark for whether AI agents given real access to a person's accounts keep acting in that person's interest when the content they're processing is adversarial. There's a v0.1 built already. Thanks, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Idris — asked two process questions that are useful either way. No commitment made.
